Gram-quantities of earth-abundant Cu single-atom anchored on N-doped porous carbons were synthesized via a facile and scalable method. The as-prepared catalyst exhibits exceptional CO2 electroreduction to CO performance. The atomically dispersed Cu-N4 structures are responsible for the highly efficient, selective and stable CO production.

Abstract：Developing efficient, selective, and stable single-atom electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is attractive but still remains a challenging, especially for scalable production with low-cost. Among the non-precious metal single-atom electrocatalysts, Cu single-atom electrocatalysts are rarely explored for the efficient CO2-to-CO conversion. Herein, we reported a facile and scalable strategy to prepare the Cu single-atom catalyst (Cu SAs/NC) with exceptional CO production performances. Atomically dispersed Cu-N4 moieties are unambiguously verified by HAADF-STEM and XANES measurements. The as-prepared Cu SAs/NC catalyst delivers a high CO faradaic efficiency of 92% at -0.7 VRHE as well as the excellent durability over 30 h successive electrolysis. It should be noted that this is one of the rare examples of efficient CO production on Cu single-atom electrocatalyst. Besides, the 20-gram+ samples can be readily fabricated in one batch and exhibit the almost identical CO2RR performances. Furthermore, the combined experimental and theoretical calculation results identify the genuine active Cu-N4 sites are responsible for the high selectivity and efficiency of CO production. This work provides a novel strategy for scalable single-atom electrocatalysts in stable quality and offers new insights into the efficient CO2-to-CO conversion on Cu single-atom electrocatalyst.
Keywords: CO2 electroreduction; Scalable production; Cu single-atoms, CO2-to-CO conversion

sections.heading: Introduction.
sections.text:
The extensive utilization of fossil fuels accelerates the accumulation of carbon dioxide (CO2) to over 420 ppm in the atmosphere and projected to be 570 ppm by 2100 [1,2]. Electroreduction of CO2 into value-added fuels and chemicals by using renewable and intermittent electricity is a particularly appealing strategy to alleviate the environment crisis as well as meet the ever-increasing energy demands [3,4]. However, the inertness of CO2 molecules and the complicated multi-electron transfer process create a large CO2 activation energy barrier to produce CO2 ·- radicals and result in the sluggish CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) kinetics [4]. In addition, the inevitable competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) further limits the efficiency and selectivity of CO2 reduction in aqueous electrolytes [5]. Therefore, exploring efficient, low-cost, and durable electrocatalyst is of great significance to steer CO2RR toward desired products with high selectivity.
Carbon monoxide (CO), as one of the most important products from CO2RR, finds many applications in chemical manufacturings and is the critical feedstock for the water-gas shift reaction and Fischer-Tropsch process [6,7]. To date, metals and their derivatives (e.g., metal oxides and metal chalcogenides) have been widely evaluated in the electroreduction of CO2 to CO [8]. Generally, Au, Ag, and Pd showed high Faradaic Efficiency (FE) for CO2-to-CO conversion, in which the tightly bonded *COOH and easily release of *CO intermediates are the two key processes [6,8]. Recently, emerging single-metal atoms confined in N-containing carbon matrixes (M-N-C) catalysts not only endow the maximum metal utilization, but also significantly improve the catalytic activity and stability [9,10]. The N atom features one more electron in the valence shell than C atoms and, thus can anchor and stabilize the atomically dispersed metal ions [11,12]. Earth-abundant and non-noble M-N-C catalysts (M = Ni, Fe, and Co) have been demonstrated to exhibit favorable FE for CO production (FECO) above 90% in CO2RR under ambient conditions [13-15]. However, the efficient CO2-to-CO conversion on Cu-N-C catalyst is rarely reported and remains largely unexplored due to the moderate *COOH adsorption and
4
sometimes difficult *CO desorption on Cu-N sites [16]. For example, Kamiya et al. prepared single Ni atoms on N-modified graphene (Ni-N-Gr) and the high activity for CO formation with a FE exceeding 90% at -0.7 ~ -0.9 VRHE was observed. In contrast, Cu-N-Gr only showed an inferior FECO below 20% over the entire overpotential range [17].
In addition, preventing the atomically dispersed metal atoms with high surface energy from migration and agglomeration is still very challenging. The synthetic methods can be clarified into two categories, one is atomically surface engineering, including atomic layer deposition, atomic layer tripping, etc. [18,19]; another one is templating method, involving the utilization of sacrificing scaffolds such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), graphene, or carbon nanotube templates [17,20,21]. These methods are inviable for the scale-up production due to their time-consuming and high-cost. Therefore, developing facile and scalable strategies to prepare M-N-C catalysts is highly desirable and urgent.
Herein, we report a facile and scalable production strategy of single Cu atoms dispersed on N-doped carbon substrate (Cu SAs/NC) catalyst with high-performance CO2-to-CO conversion. The defect-rich carbon hosts via pyrolysis of nitrogen-doped renewable chitosan can trap and stabilize isolated Cu atoms during the one-pot thermal activation. Moreover, this method can be readily and stably magnified to produce gram-scale catalyst in laboratory. As a result, the as-synthesized Cu SAs/NC catalyst exhibits an impressive FECO of 92% at -0.7 VRHE as well as superior long-term stability over 30 h. Moreover, density functional theory (DFT) calculation and poisoning experiments have confirmed that the formed Cu-N4 sites are responsible for the excellent CO2-to-CO catalytic performances. The detailed Gibbs free-energy comparisons have illustrated the origin of superior CO production. This work provides a novel and efficient scalable method to prepare Cu-N-C catalysts.

5
characterization, and measurements. Detailed materials and methods are provided in Supplement Materials.
Synthesis of Catalyst. Typically, chitosan was carbonized at 400 for 1 h with a heating rate of 5 min-1 in a tube furnace under N2 atmosphere. Then, 2.0 g carbonized chitosan, 2.0 g KOH, and 1.0 g CuCl2·2H2O were dissolved in deionized water (80 mL) and vigorously stirred for 12 h. The solution was evaporated until a slurry formed and further heated to 900 in a tube furnace under N2 atmosphere for 1 h with a heating rate of 5 min-1. The obtained black power was dispersed into a 1 M HCl solution with refluxing at 120 for 12 h to remove metal residue, followed by deionized water washing and collected by filtrating (characterizations of catalysts before HCl etching were supplied in Supplement Materials). The obtained sample is denoted as Cu SAs/NC. For comparison, Cu NPs/NC and NC were also fabricated via the same procedure but with 4.0 g CuCl2·2H2O and without CuCl2·H2O addition, respectively.
Characterization Methods. Linear sweep voltammograms (LSV) and potentiostatic electrolysis were performed on a CHI 630E electrochemical workstation (Shanghai Chenhua). The gaseous products in the cathodic compartment were analyzed by on-line gas chromatography (GC, Agilent, 7890B), liquid products in the catholyte were quantified using 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR, Bruker, Advance 600) with water suppression by a pre-saturation method. The FE of products was calculated based on their concentrations as previously described [22]. The morphology was demonstrated using filed-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, FEI New Generation Nava Nano SEM450, Netherlands) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) with Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis (Talos F200X microscope, Netherlands). Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images were performed with a JEOL ARM 200F microscope (Japan) at 200 kV. The contents of Cu and K were measured by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES, optima 8000,
6
America). X-ray diffraction patterns (XRD) were identified using a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.5406 Å). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) tests were conducted with a monochromated Al Kα excitation source (Thermo Fisher Scientific, ESCALEAB 250Xi, America). The C and N contents were quantified by an elemental analyzer (Elementar Vario MICRO, Germany). Raman spectra were performed on a Confocal LabRam HR800 spectrometer with 473 nm radiation (HORIBA Jobin Yvon, France). The X-ray absorption fine-structure (XAFS) spectra were collected on the beamline BL01C1 in National Synchrotron Radiation Research Center (NSRRC). The radiation was monochromatized by a Si (111) double-crystal monochromator. The Cu K-edge XANES data were recorded in a fluorescence mode. The textural properties were assessed by N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms at 77 K (Micromeritics ASAP 2460, America). The 13C isotopic labeling experiments were performed and analyzed via a Clarus 600 mass spectrometer (Perkin Elmer, USA).

sections.heading: Results and discussion
sections.text:
The atomically isolated Cu SAs/NC catalyst was prepared via one-pot pyrolysis
of chitosan, KOH, and Cu salt. Chitosan with naturally rich N content was converted into the defect-rich carbon substrate that stably entraps single Cu atoms via the charge transfer mechanism [23]. Meanwhile, KOH, as the activation agent, creates abundant interconnected pores and channels to facilitate the electrolyte infiltration [24,25]. The metal-free NC matrix displays a honeycomb morphology with abundant worm-like micropores (Figure S2). The significant morphological transformation was observed with CuCl2 addition as Cu SAs/NC exhibits a cross-linked structure with numerous intersectional channels (Figure 1a). The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image (Figure 1b) reveals the thin sheet-like morphology without aggregation of Cu nanoparticles. The corresponding ring-like selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern (Figure 1b insert) and high-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) image (Figure 1c) both indicate the poor crystallinity and amorphous carbon structure. Note that the graphic microcrystalline domain, as highlighted in Figure 1c, implies that Cu doping
7
Nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms at 77 K were measured to determine the specific surface areas and pore structures. The type-I isotherms manifest the dominant microporous nature on Cu SAs/NC and NC (Figure S4a) [29]. The
8
Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) specific surface area of NC was determined to be 1450.3 m2 g-1, whereas, the BET surface areas of Cu SAs/NC and Cu NPs/NC were decreased to 610.1 and 41.0 m2 g-1, respectively, because the Cu incorporation will partially block the opening of pores and channels. Pore size distribution plots disclose that the pore sizes mostly locate at 1.3 to 3.0 nm (Figure S4b). The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns all showed two broad peaks centered at 24.5° and 44.2°, corresponding to the (002) and (100) lattice plane of amorphous carbon (Figure 2a) [24,30]. There are no visible characteristic peaks of Cu or Cu clusters even on Cu NPs/NC, due to the low loading content and high dispersion of Cu species. Raman spectra display two peaks located at 1349 cm-1 (D band) and 1596 cm-1 (G band), which represents the defective graphitic structure and symmetry-allowed graphite band, respectively (Figure S5) [25,30]. The intensity ratio of D and G band (ID/IG) quantifies the amount of defects in carbon frameworks. Concretely, the highest ID/IG value of 1.02 is observed on Cu SAs/NC and verifies its abundant defects [24,31].
Interestingly, ultimate element analysis reveals the higher N contents were observed on Cu SAs/NC (4.26 wt%) and Cu NPs/NC (5.10 wt%) than that of NC (1.64 wt%), implying that the anchored Cu atoms in N-defects can prevent the N-functionality loss and form stable Cu-N bonds. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was further conducted to probe the chemical states of Cu and N species. The high-resolution N 1s peaks can be deconvoluted into three peaks, indexing to pyridinic-N (398.1 eV), pyrrolic-N (400.7 eV), and oxidized-N (403.9 eV) on all catalysts (Figure 2b) [7,32]. Notably, the Cu-N bonds at 399.5 eV are observed on Cu SAs/NC and Cu NPs/NC, but not on NC. The content of Cu-N bonds decreased from 21.6 at.% on Cu SAs/NC to 2.3 at.% on Cu NPs/NC, indicating the dominating Cu nanoparticles instead of coordinated Cu atoms on Cu NPs/NC. Moreover, the Cu 2p3/2 peak (933.7 eV) on Cu SAs/NC locates between Cu0 (932.4 eV) and Cu2+ (934.6 eV), suggesting the valence state of Cu atoms in Cu SAs/NC is between 0 and +2 (Figure 2c). Whereas, the Cu 2p signal of Cu NPs/NC, as shown in Figure S7c, suggests the formation of CuO nanoparticles. The inductively coupled plasma optical emission
9
spectroscopy (ICP-OES) reveals that the Cu contents of 0.32 wt.% (Cu SAs/NC) and 4.17 wt.% are obtained on Cu SAs/NC and Cu NPs/NC, respectively (Table S1).
Figure 2. XRD profiles for all catalysts (a). N 1s spectra (b), and Cu 2p (c) spectra of Cu SAs/NC.
Moreover, X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES) was employed to
investigate the valence state of Cu species in Cu SAs/NC. Figure 3a indicates that Cu SAs/NC has a higher oxidation state than Cu foil but a lower oxidation state than Cu(NO3)2 solution, confirming that the Cu valence state is between 0 and +2, and agrees with XPS result. The K2-weighted Fourier transformed of Cu K-edge extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) oscillation shows a dominant peak at 1.5 Å on Cu SAs/NC (Figure 3b), which arises from the first shell Cu-N coordination. Besides, the absence of Cu-Cu path at 2.2 Å confirms the single Cu atoms dispersion on the nitrogenated carbon substrate, which is consistent with the HAADF-STEM results. Besides, the wavelet transform (WT) analysis plot was applied to distinguish the backscattering atoms [33,34]. As shown in Figure 3c, Cu SAs/NC shows the maximum WT centered at 4.6 Å−1 that is shorter than Cu-Cu (7.6 Å−1) and Cu-O (6.2
10
Å−1) bonds. Based on the EXAFS fitting results, the coordination number of N for Cu is 3.9 on Cu SAs/NC (Figure 3b insert and Table S4).
SAs/NC is expected to be an efficient CO2RR catalyst. The electrocatalytic activity of Cu SAs/NC catalyst toward CO2RR was evaluated in a three-electrode H-cell with CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte under ambient conditions. The Cu NPs/NC and NC catalysts were also evaluated as references. As illustrated by linear sweep voltammograms (LSV) curves in Figure 4a, Cu SAs/NC exhibits a low onset potential of -0.23 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE, all the potentials are referred to RHE afterword) on Cu SAs/NC, which is more positive than that on Cu NPs/NC (-0.30 V) and NC (-0.45 V). It should be noted that the onset potential on Cu SAs/NC is also more positive than most of benchmark M-N-C catalysts reported recently [11,17,35]. Meanwhile, Cu SAs/NC showed a current density of 8.9 mA cm-2 at -1.0 V,
11
which is significantly larger than that of Cu NPs/NC (5.1 mA cm-2) and NC (2.4 mA cm-2). Additionally, the much smaller current densities and higher overpotentials are observed in the N2-saturated KHCO3 electrolyte (Figures 4a insert and S8), indicating the CO2RR-stemmed electrocatalysis activity [17,20].
The potential CO2RR products were comprehensively analyzed using on-line gas chromatography (GC) and 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR). As shown in Figures 4b-d, the FEs of products are strongly dependent on the applied potentials, while H2, CO, and HCOOH are the main detected products. Cu SAs/NC exhibits a preferential activity for CO production with suppressed H2 evolution and HCOOH generation at all applied potentials, the FECO reaches up to 92% at -0.7 V with no HCOOH detected (Figures 4b and S10), suggesting the favorable CO2-to-CO selectivity. The FECO value is 5 and 12 times higher than that of Cu NPs/NC (19%) and NC (8%) at the same potential. Moreover, the performances of Cu SAs/NC catalyst is among the best-performed CO2RR catalysts, the detailed comparison is summarized in Table S5. Notably, the FECO of Cu SAs/NC decreases rapidly at more negative potentials, suggesting that HER takes over at high overpotentials [15]. The evidently inferior FEs for CO production on Cu NPs/NC demonstrate the advantages of single Cu atoms rather than Cu particles. On the other hand, the poor CO2RR performance observed on NC (Cu-free catalyst) further unambiguously confirmed the crucial role of Cu-N coordination. To confirm the origin of the CO product, the isotope labeling experiment was carried out with 13CO2 substituting for 12CO2 as feeding gas. Figure S14 depicts the signals of 13CO (m/z = 29) traced by the mass spectrometry, furthermore, the consistent current density and FE of 13CO compared with the values of 12CO (m/z = 28) firmly demonstrate that the produced CO was solely originated from CO2RR rather than the catalysts or bicarbonate ions from the electrolyte.
12
To understand the outstanding CO2RR performances, electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) was estimated from the double-layer capacitance (Figure S15). As expected, Cu SAs/NC exhibits the largest ECSA of 119 mF cm-2, which is 2.3 and 3.3 times higher than that of Cu NPs/NC and NC (Figure 5a). Despite the BET specific surface area of Cu SAs/NC is smaller than that of NC, Cu SAs/NC still showed a larger ECSA than NC due to its abundant and exposed catalytic active sites [36]. Such observation coincides with the CO2 adsorption capacity as well in Figures S16, Cu SAs/NC displays a superior CO2 uptake of 3.22 mmol g -1 at ambient conditions that significantly higher than that of Cu NPs/NC (0.45 mmol g-1) and NC (2.67 mmol g-1). Additionally, the highest CO2 isosteric heats of adsorption (Qst) of 35.4 kJ mol-1 at zero coverage observed on Cu SAs/NC presents the highest CO2 adsorption affinity as well (Figure S16d) [24,25]. The enhanced CO2 capture capacity and Qst can increase the local CO2 concentration around the catalyst/electrolyte
13
interface to compensate for the limited CO2 solubility. Reaction kinetics were analyzed by means of Tafel plots on different catalysts. As shown in Figure 5b, Cu SAs/NC possesses a Tafel slope of 115 mV dec-1 that is lower than the 151 and 163 mV dec-1 obtained on Cu NPs/NC and NC, respectively. This implies the faster first proton-coupled electron transfer step on Cu SAs/NC compared to the reference samples, and confirms that the generation of *COOH intermediate is the rate-determining step [20,37].
The active center of Cu SAs/NC was also confirmed by the poisoning experiment as the SCN- ions can chelate metal ions to devitalize the metal center in M-N-C catalysts [38,39]. The Cu SAs/NC was dispersed within a 0.01 M KSCN solution for 30 min, as a result, a striking depression of FECO from 92% to 35% and current density from 3.47 to 0.55 mA cm-2 were recorded on Cu SAs/NC (Figure 4c). This result unambiguously verifies that the Cu-N sites are the active centers for CO2RR. The long-term stability test was conducted at -0.7 V for 60 hours, Cu SAs/NC shows a steady current density over the consecutive CO2RR and the almost identical FECO of 92% was recorded in Figure 5d. The electrolyte after 30 hours of electrolysis was further tested by ICP-OES and no Cu content was detected. In addition, the similar XRD patterns of Cu SAs/NC before and after long-term CO2RR also indicate the excellent robustness of Cu SAs/NC (Figure S17).
Motivated by the excellent CO2 reduction performance of Cu SAs/NC as well as its low-cost and facile preparation, the scalable production trial was conducted in our laboratory. As shown in Figure 5e, 22.8 g Cu SAs/NC catalyst can be prepared in one batch. The activity of the resultant catalyst for CO2RR was also measured, a high FECO of 91% and a current density of 3.61 mA cm -2 were recorded on massive-produced Cu SAs/NC catalyst, which are almost identical to the pristine Cu SAs/NC (Figure 5f). These outstanding results indicate the synthesis strategy can be readily and stably scaled up.
14
To uncover the high performances and selectivity of Cu SAs/NC catalyst for CO2-to-CO conversion, first principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed. The model of Cu-N4 moiety embedded in graphene nanosheet was constructed based on the Cu-N coordination number of 3.9 determined by EXAFS fitting result. The adsorption and reaction free energies of key intermediates in CO2RR are calculated. It is notable that the selectivity toward CO production is almost 100% (Figure S11). In other words, the alternative reaction pathways (Figures
15
S18) for the intermediates of *CHO, *COH, and *COCO generation are inhibited or thermodynamically unfavorable [6,40]. As shown in Figure 6a, the highest free-energy for the formation of *COH (2.83 eV) was required, followed by *COCO (1.04 eV) and *CHO (0.87 eV). In contrast, the free-energy of releasing *CO to produce CO is an initiative. These results are consistent with the experimental observations that the CO2 is inclined to form CO with high selectivity.
Furthermore, the proposed reaction pathway of CO2-to-CO conversion and free-energies are illustrated in Figure 6b. The proton-coupled electron transfer step of CO2→*COOH is suggested to be the rate-determining step (RDS) since it exhibited the largest uphill energy barrier of 1.65 eV. Similarly, free energy change of the key *OCHO intermediate for HCOOH generation was also calculated (Figure 6c), a higher value of 1.72 eV indicates the unfavorable HCOOH formation that is consistent with the experimental results. The subsequent *COOH to *CO generation in CO formation proceeds an exergonic downhill, further confirming the easy conversion of *COOH to *CO. This is in line with the previous reports that the *COOH → *CO process is typically facile [16,41]. The following *CO desorption step on Cu-N4 exhibits the negative free-energy (0.96 eV), revealing that the *CO intermediates could be easily and facilely released from the catalyst surface and tend to CO production. The electronic structures were analyzed to gain deep insights into the interaction between the crucial *COOH intermediate and catalytic active sites. As depicted in the calculated charge density difference diagram (Figure 6c), the accumulated electrons occurred around the Cu-C bond indicates the strong attraction between the catalytic surface and *COOH. According to the metal-ligand bonding theory of organometallic catalysts, the main interactions between the catalyst surface and the *COOH intermediate are σ-bonding and π-bonding [13,42]. Figure 6d displayed the partial density of states (PDOS) for *COOH adsorbed on Cu-N4 system, the 3d orbital of Cu atom and the 2p orbital of C atom in *COOH intermediate showed the obvious overlap, demonstrating that Cu-N4 sites can strongly stabilize the *COOH intermediates [43].
16

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, to develop the facile and scalable method for M-N-C catalysts, we
demonstrated a readily scale-up strategy from the N-rich biomass and one-pot fabrication that could produce 20-gram+ Cu-N-C catalysts from one batch with stable quality and comparatively investigated for their CO2RR performances. The single dispersed Cu atoms were clearly verified by the HAADF-STEM, XPS, and XANES measurements. The as-synthesized Cu SAs/NC catalyst exhibited an exceptional FECO of 92% at -0.7 V. It should be noted that it is the very first example of CO2-to-CO conversion achieved on the Cu-N-C catalyst. Moreover, the current density and selectivity were stably retained for successive electrolysis for 30 h. The origin of CO
17
was further confirmed by the 13C isotope labeling experiments. The genuine active sites were illustrated by the DFT calculation and poisoning experiments. The high selectivity and favorable energy formation of CO were systematically evaluated. This work provides a novel and scalable method to produce M-N-C catalysts and provides new insights into the efficient CO2-to-CO conversion on Cu-N-C catalysts.
